hops.title: Zebrafish with a spare set of escape neurons
hops.text: A larval zebrafish has one giant escape neuron on each side of rhombomere 4. A touch to its tail can trigger one of them to fire, bending the fish into a fast C-shape away. In 2004 Melina Hale, Victoria Prince and colleagues at the University of Chicago studied larvae in which a Hox gene switched on out of place had produced extra giant neurons two segments forward, in r2. Were the extras just look-alikes? The team used a laser to remove the normal r4 neuron on one side, then startled the fish again. The first bend was still about as sharp and fast. The r2 copy could do the job.

sources.citation: Hale ME, Kheirbek MA, Schriefer JE, Prince VE. Hox gene misexpression and cell-specific lesions reveal functionality of homeotically transformed neurons. Journal of Neuroscience 24(12):3070-3076 (2004)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A translucent zebrafish larva curving sharply through clear water away from a ripple.
image.caption: A changed Hox code gave zebrafish larvae a working backup escape neuron two segments forward.

hops.title: Families with a HOXB1 change
hops.text: Sixteen years after mice lacking Hoxb1 were shown to fail to form a normal facial motor nucleus, a similar pattern turned up in people. In 2012 Bryn Webb, Elizabeth Engle, Ethylin Jabs and colleagues described four people in two German-American families, all with facial weakness on both sides from birth and hearing loss. All four had first been diagnosed with Moebius syndrome, but none had the limited outward eye movement that diagnosis requires. Each carried the same change in both copies of HOXB1: a cysteine in place of an arginine that grips DNA. By 2021, seventeen people in six families were known.

sources.citation: Webb BD et al. HOXB1 founder mutation in humans recapitulates the phenotype of Hoxb1-/- mice. American Journal of Human Genetics 91(1):171-179 (2012)
Webb BD, Manoli I, Engle EC, Jabs EW. A cranial nerve developmental disorder caused by HOXB1 variants (review). Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases 16:173 (2021)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small brown mouse sitting on a lab bench beside a rack of sample tubes and a pipette.
image.caption: People with a harmful HOXB1 variant in both copies show facial weakness like that of Hoxb1 knockout mice.

hops.title: Why too many carrots turn palms orange
hops.text: Too much vitamin A can disturb an early embryo, making carrots look suspicious. Carrots carry beta-carotene; the fraction converted to vitamin A falls as intake rises, and dietary beta-carotene has not been shown to cause vitamin A toxicity. With sustained excessive intake, unconverted pigment tints palms and soles a harmless yellow-orange; a 1942 wartime series included a jaundice referral. Preformed vitamin A skips that step. A 1995 study of 22,748 pregnancies linked high early intake to defects in structures formed partly from cranial neural crest; a later case-control study found no clear link at overlapping supplement intakes. Conventional oral beta-carotene did not cause birth defects in rats or rabbits.
